items.title: Nvidia reportedly halts chip shipments to south-east Asia as stock sell-off eases – business live
items.summary:
UK competition watchdog finds millions of people can’t afford private dental care, with prices rising by an inflation-busting 7% a year

Dental care is the medical treatment Brits are most likely to put off because of high costs, a separate report found this week – forcing some people to do their own dentristy.

Drawing on what people wrote about their care in UK forum threads, a new study by the private clinic Zental Dental set out to find which treatments people delay when they cannot cover the cost, and the dentist came up more than any other treatment.

Dental care is the medical treatment Brits most often delay or skip for financial reasons, with dental prices up 29% since 2021.

Glasses were in second place. Prices for glasses and contact lenses climbed 21% from September 2021 to September 2026. A pair of varifocals can cost as much as £500.

Switching to a cheaper option rather than going without is most common with prescriptions, a step 39 of 65 people took.

Some variation is to be expected, but the CMA is concerned that people are paying more than they should because they are unable to shop around.

Continue reading...

items.title: ‘Look what I’ve produced’: Inside ‘peacock parenting,’ where kids become their parents’ status symbols
items.summary:
Today’s parents are consciously trying to break with how they were raised, prioritizing emotional well-being over punitive discipline. But a parenting phenomenon gaining attention seems at odds with that generational shift : “peacock parenting,” in which children become status symbols for their parents.

In ZERO TO THREE’s First Voice survey of more than 2,200 parents of children ages 5 and under, conducted this summer, 61% say they tell their kids “I love you” more often than their own parents did. Sixty percent say they focus more on their children’s mental health, and 56% say they won’t use the physical discipline they experienced growing up.

Peacock parenting describes a pattern of narcissistic behavior in which parents prioritize their own need for admiration and control over their children’s emotional needs. There’s no prevalence data specific to the term, and the underlying psychology is not new. What has changed is the public visibility of children’s lives, and the opportunities for parents to turn their kids’ achievements into social and financial capital.

Parenting has a new report card 

“Pride says, ‘I’m so happy for you.’ Peacocking says, ‘look what I’ve produced,’” says Dr. Christine Ghilain, a double board-certified clinical neuropsychologist and founder of Brain Health Neuropsychology in New Jersey. “It tips over when the moment is for the audience and not the child.”

She says the red flags include an achievement that doesn’t feel real until it’s been posted, moments staged or redone for the camera, repeated posting even after a child objects, and a…
items.t: ‘Look what I’ve produced’: Inside ‘peacock parenting,’ where kids become their parents’ status symbols

items.title: ‘Businesses hate chaos’: $166 billion in tariff refunds are flowing to companies, not the customers who paid
items.summary:
American companies are collecting roughly $166 billion in tariff refunds, plus interest, for costs that many consumers helped pay. Some of that money is going to bonuses.

At least nine public companies have disclosed using part of their refunds for executive or employee bonuses, according to a ProPublica investigation that used an AI tool to analyze securities filings and earnings calls. They include TJX , the owner of T.J. Maxx and Marshalls; Acushnet, which owns the golf brand Titleist; and the toolmaker Stanley Black & Decker.

TJX has set aside $167 million of its $463 million in refunds for incentive pay and discretionary bonuses for non-executive associates, according to its third-quarter earnings release , as Fortune reported last week . That is about 3% of the $5.5 billion TJX earned in its last fiscal year.

Acushnet disclosed that about $12 million of its $45.8 million in refunds would go to incentive compensation. Stanley Black & Decker, which is getting at least $298 million according to ProPublica’s refund database , hasn’t said how much will fund bonuses.

The money is landing with importers rather than the customers who absorbed higher prices, and few precedents exist for a scale like this.

“I think it’s fair to say that at this scale, it’s unprecedented, partly because the scale of business right now is unlike what we’ve seen in prior years,” Kathleen Claussen, a law professor at Georgetown University, told Fortune .

How emergency tariffs turned into a refund windfall 

In February 2025, President Donald Trump declared a national emergency over illegal…
items.t: ‘Businesses hate chaos’: $166 billion in tariff refunds are flowing to companies, not the customers who paid

items.title: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way
items.summary:
As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows , a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

“ Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest , tells Fortune . “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”

Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through cloud platform Vercel went to open-weight models , up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.” 

Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

The case for ‘good enough’ AI 

Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream…
items.t: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

items.title: They were in high school when ChatGPT arrived and in college when their friends got accused of cheating. Now their AI software polices 40 colleges
items.summary:
When OpenAI released ChatGPT on Nov. 30, 2022, Derin Suzener was a high school senior already leaning toward a career in AI. He got there “without having taken a single computer science course back in 11th grade,” he told Fortune . “I did not start using ChatGPT until I entered university, actually.”

Nikita Kravcenko, his future cofounder, was also in high school, taking AP classes where “my teachers were bombarding students with anti-AI policy, because it was like a new technology at that point,” he said. “So they were very fearful of what it could do and write. So they were essentially having a craze over it.”

By the time they got to Purdue, the craze had casualties. “I was seeing all of my friends get accused of cheating with AI on their computer science assignments,” Suzener said. “And they would have a pretty hard time proving it, actually.”

So Suzener, Kravcenko and two classmates built a way to prove it. Their company, Remora, makes Syntax, a document editor that records how a student writes a paper (typing speed, cursor movement, what gets pasted in) and flags anything odd for the teacher to review. The founders say it’s used in classrooms at 40 U.S. colleges and universities, though they declined to name any, saying that identifying customers could help larger competitors go after the same schools. The company says four more institutions will start using it next semester. Students can also buy it themselves, starting at $9.99 for three months.

The pitch is protection for students who did their own work. “The guilty are truly proven to be guilty, and then the…
items.t: They were in high school when ChatGPT arrived and in college when their friends got accused of cheating. Now their AI software polices 40 colleges

items.title: Forget petrodollars, ‘chip-dollars’ show U.S. power now flows from tech dominance—but the new currency regime is ‘inherently riskier,’ analyst says
items.summary:
Semiconductors are surpassing oil as the linchpin of the dollar’s global reach, demonstrating U.S. technological might but also revealing a less stable foundation, according to Deutsche Bank .

In a note last week, foreign exchange strategist Mallika Sachdeva pointed out that for the first time in modern history, global trade in chips now exceeds trade in oil and gas. Excluding China, Asia’s surplus in the chip trade matches petroleum-related surpluses in the Persian Gulf, she added.

That’s as AI hyperscalers keep ramping up capital expenditures, which are expected to top $1 trillion next year, further propping up chip trade flows.

“The rise of chips as a driver of dollar dominance can be seen as a symptom of change in the ultimate source of U.S. power — from geopolitical to technological leadership,” Sachdeva wrote, adding that the so-called petrodollar is quickly being superseded by the new “chip-dollar.”

The petrodollar regime goes back to a deal struck in 1974 when Saudi Arabia agreed to price its oil in dollars and invest surpluses in U.S. assets, especially Treasury debt. In return, the American military ensured security in the region and free navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And because oil is a core input to global manufacturing and transport, supply chains have a natural incentive to dollarize. Indeed, Mideast oil and gas are used to make petrochemicals, fertilizer, and even helium.

But the underpinnings of the petrodollar are breaking down due to the Iran war as Tehran exposes the limits of the U.S. military, while the AI boom is sending a tsunami of…
items.t: Forget petrodollars, ‘chip-dollars’ show U.S. power now flows from tech dominance—but the new currency regime is ‘inherently riskier,’ analyst says

items.title: The AI boom helped lift retirement accounts, but the Nvidia whiplash showed how much investors’ financial futures depend on a handful of stocks
items.summary:
Millions of Americans, and their financial futures, may be exposed to the recent AI-fueled swings in the market regardless of whether they’ve ever used a chatbot.

Stocks plunged Wednesday morning before recovering much of the loss. Near the start of trading, the Dow fell more than 1,000 points and the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% as AI chip stocks sold off for a second straight day. Nvidia fell as much as 8%. By late afternoon, the S&P 500 had cut its loss to about half a percent, and the Dow had turned higher.

Wednesday’s swing capped a week in which a single company’s board decision moved the index that holds much of Americans’ retirement accounts. Roughly two-thirds of of Fidelity 401(k) savers keep everything in a target-date fund. 

Following a tumultuous few weeks in which Jensen Huang resigned and was later reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaker’s stock jumped 31%, added about $950 billion in market value, and lifted the S&P 500 by 4.7%. Still, the S&P 500 is now about 8% below its Oct. 6 record. Last Friday it closed 11.6% below that high, putting it in correction territory, after seven straight losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

Stock market concentration has been on the rise for years, and it is now near 35-year highs. Just 10 stocks in the S&P 500 account for about 39% of its total market capitalization, with the five largest stocks—all tech giants—alone accounting for 29%, according to Charles Schwab . That means an American with $100,000 in an index fund tied to the S&P 500 would have $29,000 in just five stocks.

As a result, many…
items.t: The AI boom helped lift retirement accounts, but the Nvidia whiplash showed how much investors’ financial futures depend on a handful of stocks

items.title: GTA VI was built by hand. The man who ran Take-Two during GTA IV says AI could let a filmmaker make the next breakout game
items.summary:
Grand Theft Auto VI , on track to be the biggest entertainment launch of any kind, was made the old-fashioned way: Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said in February that Rockstar Games built the game without generative AI.

“With regards to GTA 6, generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building. Their worlds are handcrafted. That’s what differentiates them,” Zelnick told GamesIndustry.biz . “They’re built from the ground up, building by building, street by street, neighborhood by neighborhood.”

That’s not to say it didn’t take time and money. Analysts estimate Take-Two spent more than a billion dollars on the game, which came out more than 13 years after its predecessor (Zelnick never confirmed the amount but admitted the game was “expensive”). But the next blockbuster video game might come sooner, cheaper—and with an even more cinematic lens, according to Ben Feder, who ran Take-Two Interactive when Grand Theft Auto IV came out in 2008 .

“Some great creative mind who would have otherwise gone to make a film will make a video game because it’s as simple as point and click,” Feder said in a long and winding conversation with Fortune about the state of the entertainment industry.

Feder, now managing partner of Tirta Ventures, said in a Fortune commentary this month that AI will change how big games get made. His firm invests in AI-native game projects . “We put our money where our mouth is,” he said of Tirta’s investments.

Ben Feder, managing partner at Tirta Ventures and former CEO of Take-Two Interactive. Courtesy of Ben Feder 

The next great…
items.t: GTA VI was built by hand. The man who ran Take-Two during GTA IV says AI could let a filmmaker make the next breakout game

items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

items.title: L.A. Lakers announce deal with Kalshi, signaling sports leagues’ growing embrace of prediction markets
items.summary:
The Los Angeles Lakers have announced a tie-up with Kalshi, becoming the latest sports team to partner with a prediction market—and leaving little doubt about where the National Basketball Association has placed its chips in the ongoing debate about the role of the controversial wagering platforms in the world of pro sports. The team announced the news on Tuesday in a brief statement that hailed the partnership, but offered few details on what it will entail. 

“We’re excited … to explore innovative ways to engage fans and strengthen their connection to the game,” said Los Angeles Lakers president and chief business officer Lon Rosen. 

The announcement also solidified a broader alliance between the NBA and prediction markets. The league officially embraced the platforms only a month ago, when it named Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred exchanges. Kalshi has since moved quickly to turn that opening into team-level agreements, signing the Philadelphia 76ers in October before adding the Lakers this week. 

The NBA’s overall positioning came as something of a surprise, given that it and the National Football League had largely held back while other major sports leagues signed agreements with prediction markets. Some of these platforms let users as young as 18 wager on event contracts, with sports making up the bulk of trading.

Other major sports organizations have mostly taken a welcoming approach. The National Hockey League became the first major North American professional sports league to strike prediction market deals in October 2025, signing multiyear agreements with…
items.t: L.A. Lakers announce deal with Kalshi, signaling sports leagues’ growing embrace of prediction markets

items.title: How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era
items.summary:
The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem. It marked the end of a 15-year arrangement with U.S. chipmaker Qualcomm , whose chips had been used in every iPhone since the iPhone 4, excluding some of Apple’s budget “e” series, to connect the devices to a mobile network. 

“You take us out, and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, says, explaining how its chips work. 

While he adds that the company knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints. 

In the year to September, Qualcomm’s total revenue fell 3% to $43.1 billion. Chip sales were down 26%, in the final three months to September. 

McGuire argues the loss of Apple leaves Qualcomm less exposed to a single customer. “It’s actually very freeing when you can rebalance your customer ecosystem,” he says. In his view, Qualcomm’s success does not hinge on whether its chips end up in one phone maker’s handsets. “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.” 

The company has meanwhile sought expansion beyond the smartphone category into the laptop, car, smart-home device, wearables, and data center markets. Revenue outside of Qualcomm’s mobile chip business is anticipated to grow by more than 60% in 2027. 

Data centers remain a lucrative market for chipmakers, but it’s currently dominated by Nvidia , whose data center…
items.t: How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era

items.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
items.summary:
Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge

In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.

That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

items.title: After $26 billion in gifts, MacKenzie Scott is still worth $27 billion—and just gave Atlanta students $8 million more
items.summary:
Four years ago, MacKenzie Scott gave $8 million to Achieve Atlanta, a nonprofit that helps Atlanta public school students pay for and finish college. Last week, the organization announced she had done it again , with a second $8 million gift that brings her total support to $16 million.

It is one of two gifts Scott made to Georgia education nonprofits this month, together worth $12.5 million. The donor has given away more than $26 billion since her 2019 divorce from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, yet is still worth more than $27 billion, largely because Amazon stock keeps rising.

For an Atlanta Public Schools graduate pursuing a bachelor’s degree, the need-based Achieve Atlanta scholarship can be worth up to $20,000 over four years . Students at two-year colleges and in technical programs can receive $1,500 a year for up to four semesters.

The nonprofit also helps students choose colleges, work through the application process, and find their first jobs. Since 2015, it has awarded more than $75 million in scholarships.

An independent evaluation by researchers affiliated with Georgia State University’s Georgia Policy Labs found that 91% of Achieve Atlanta scholars returned for a second semester of college. Among peers who also graduated from Atlanta Public Schools, had similar academic and demographic backgrounds, and enrolled in college without the program’s support, 77% did.

The gap narrows over time but holds. Six years after high school, 42% of scholars had graduated, compared with 36% of similar peers.

items.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot
items.summary:
Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

items.title: Compass’s logic for US listing is flimsy but UK ministers need to wake up to Footsie flight risk | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting?

That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028.

Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous.

items.title: Trump, Nvidia and power: could we be nearing the end of tech’s Gilded Age?
items.summary:
Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over

  • Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?

One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board reinstated Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.

But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward Folarin Balogun after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.
